practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the meaning of 'reconciliation'?

A) Punishing someone for wrongdoing
B) Restoring harmony between people who have been in conflict
C) Using violence to achieve a political goal
D) Following the rules of a just war
practice_questions.marks: B) Restoring harmony between people who have been in conflict [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give one religious teaching about peace.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for one correct teaching. Answers may include:
• 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God' (Matthew 5:9)
• As-Salaam is one of Allah's 99 names, meaning 'the source of peace'
• Muslims greet each other with 'salaam alaikum' (peace be upon you)
• Jesus taught 'love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you' (Matthew 5:44)
[1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two similar religious beliefs in contemporary British society about forgiveness.
In your answer you must refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include two of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity teaches that forgiveness is essential — Jesus said 'If you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you' (Matthew 6:14). Forgiveness is a duty for Christians.
• Similarly, Islam teaches that forgiveness brings reward from Allah — 'Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah' (Qur'an 42:40). Muslims are encouraged to forgive because Allah is 'the most forgiving'.
• Both religions teach that forgiveness can lead to reconciliation and the restoration of relationships.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about why violence is wrong.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — Jesus taught 'If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also' (Matthew 5:39), showing that Christians should not respond to violence with more violence. This reflects the broader Christian teaching that peace and love should guide all human actions.
• Islam — the Qur'an teaches 'Do not take life, which God has made sacred' (6:151), showing that Muslims believe human life has a God-given value that violence violates. While self-defence is permitted, unprovoked violence is forbidden.
• Source of authority: the Sermon on the Mount (Christianity) / the Qur'an (Islam) as a direct revelation from God.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'There is no difference between the Christian and Muslim attitudes to violence.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious arguments
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Both religions teach that peace is a core value — Christianity through Jesus's teaching on peacemaking, Islam through Allah's name As-Salaam.
• Both condemn terrorism and the targeting of innocent civilians.
• Both accept that violence may be justified in extreme circumstances, such as self-defence or as a last resort.
• Both teach the sanctity of life — violence against innocent people is always wrong.

Arguments against:
• Christianity has a stronger pacifist tradition — Jesus taught 'turn the other cheek' and the Quakers reject all violence absolutely.
• Islam permits armed struggle (lesser jihad) under strict conditions, which goes further than most Christian traditions in accepting the use of force.
• The concept of lesser jihad has no direct equivalent in mainstream Christianity.
• Some Christians argue that the Old Testament shows God supporting violence, while others reject this as outdated.

Conclusion: While there are significant similarities in their commitment to peace and condemnation of unjustified violence, there are genuine differences in how each religion frames the conditions under which force may be acceptable.
[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about reconciliation.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — Christians believe that God reconciled humanity to himself through the death of Jesus on the cross. St Paul wrote: 'God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ' (2 Corinthians 5:19). This shows that reconciliation is at the heart of the Christian faith.
• Islam — the Qur'an teaches 'Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah' (42:40). Muslims believe that restoring broken relationships pleases Allah and that reconciliation is a form of worship.
• Source of authority: the Bible / the Qur'an as the word of God.
[6 marks]

lessons.title: Peacemaking and Responses to Victims of War

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the meaning of 'peacemaking'?
A) Refusing to fight in a war
B) Working to bring about peace and end conflict
C) Giving money to charity
D) Praying for victims of war
practice_questions.marks: B — Working to bring about peace and end conflict [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give one way in which religious believers help victims of war.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for one correct way, such as:
• Pray for victims of war
• Campaign for their government to provide support to victims
• Help victims of war directly, by giving clothing, food, or shelter
• Give money to charities so that they can help the victims of war
• Provide education or healthcare to those affected
• Support refugees displaced by conflict

practice_questions.text:
Explain two different religious beliefs in contemporary British society about peacemaking.
In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point (maximum 4 marks). If the two beliefs are not contrasting, maximum 2 marks.
• Some Christians, such as Quakers, believe all conflict should be resolved peacefully. Jesus said ‘Blessed are the peacemakers’ (Matthew 5:9), meaning those who work for peace are closest to God. They refused to fight in wars but served as mediators and medics instead.
• Some Muslims believe that while peace is preferred, sometimes fighting is necessary to establish peace. The Qur’an permits self-defence (‘Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms’) but also teaches ‘if they incline towards peace, you must also incline towards it’ (Qur’an 8:61).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about the importance of peace-making in the world.
Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point, 1 mark for relevant reference to scripture (maximum 6 marks). If only one belief is mentioned, maximum 2 marks + 1 mark for scriptural reference.
• Christians believe peacemaking is central to following Jesus’ example. Jesus said ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God’ (Matthew 5:9). This means Christians who actively work for peace are carrying out God’s will and will be rewarded.
• Muslims believe that peace is fundamental to Islam, as the word Islam shares a root with ‘salam’, meaning peace. The Qur’an says ‘Making peace is better’ (Surah 4:128) and teaches that Muslims must not refuse peace when it is offered. This shows that working for peace is a religious duty.

practice_questions.text:
'Religious organisations do more to help victims of war than any other groups.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you:
• should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement
• should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• should refer to religious arguments
• may refer to non-religious arguments
• should reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Low band (1-3): One argument with justification.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Different arguments for and against with justification, OR several linked justified arguments for one position.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good well-justified arguments for and against, linked together.
Top band (10-12): Very well argued, well-justified arguments for and against, linked together and leading to a reasonable conclusion.
Arguments for:
• Christian Aid provides food, water, education, healthcare, and shelter to victims in Syria and South Sudan — motivated by Jesus’ teaching in the Parable of the Sheep and Goats
• Islamic charities channel zakah funds to provide emergency relief and rebuild communities
• Religious motivation means sustained, long-term commitment rather than short-term response
• Pope Francis has actively negotiated between conflicting parties
Arguments against:
• Secular organisations like the Red Cross and UN agencies provide the largest scale humanitarian relief
• Governments have the most resources and power to help victims through foreign aid and refugee resettlement
• Some argue religious organisations can be selective in who they help
• Non-religious charities like Médecins Sans Frontières work in the most dangerous conflict zones

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious teachings about victims of war.
Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point, 1 mark for relevant reference to scripture (maximum 6 marks). If only one belief is mentioned, maximum 2 marks + 1 mark for scriptural reference.
• Christians believe they have a duty to help victims of war because Jesus taught that helping others is the same as helping God. In the Parable of the Sheep and the Goats, Jesus said ‘Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me’ (Matthew 25:40). Those who help others will go to heaven.
• Muslims believe that saving a life is one of the highest moral acts. The Qur’an teaches ‘Whoever has saved a life, it is as though he has saved the whole of mankind’ (Surah 5:32). This motivates Muslims to protect and support those whose lives are at risk because of war.
